cards.title: The complexity of reachability for two-dimensional branching VASS
cards.formal: Determine the computational complexity of reachability for a two-dimensional branching vector addition system with states and binary-encoded numerical data. The decidability part of the original question is settled; the remaining target is the complexity classification, whose required time/space precision is not specified in the source.
cards.why: Two counters are the first dimensional increase beyond the known one-counter complexity classification. Determining the cost of exact reachability would separate the power of a terminating symbolic procedure from usable bounds on resources needed to analyze branching computations.
cards.status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. The original decidability conjecture is settled by the published MFCS 2025 theorem. The broader request for precise two-dimensional complexity remains open in the checked sources: MFCS 2025 explicitly supplies no upper bound, FoSSaCS 2026 confirms the distinction, and the July 2026 general-decidability preprint also leaves complexity bounds open. The whole card is therefore not marked resolved. No independent proof audit was performed.

progress.text: Figueira and coauthors prove PSPACE completeness in dimension one with binary displacements and ask for two-dimensional decidability and precise complexity.
Bizière, Hilaire, Leroux and Sutre prove effective semilinearity and decidability in dimension two; Section 8 explicitly leaves complexity upper bounds open.
Bizière, Leroux and Sutre give another effective-semilinearity argument in two dimensions and distinguish it from the known one-dimensional complexity classification.
The general BVAS-decidability preprint still gives no complexity upper bound; its broader claim was read but not independently verified.

sentences: A branching counter-system run combines two child configurations by adding their counters and a transition displacement.
Reachability asks whether a given configuration has a finite run tree rooted there and ending in allowed zero-counter leaves.
The 2017 question concerns the complexity of this task with two counters and binary numerical data.
Decidability was proved in 2025, but the checked sources leave an explicit complexity classification open.
This revision preserves that remaining question and marks the source’s unspecified requirement for matching time or space bounds.

cards.definitions: Use the direct two-counter extension of the 2017 model. An instance consists of a nonempty finite state set Q={1,…,s}, a finite transition list Δ⊆Q×Q×ℤ²×Q, initial states I⊆Q, and a target (q,v)∈Q×ℕ², with ℕ={0,1,2,…}. A transition (q_L,q_R,z,q_P) combines child configurations (q_L,u) and (q_R,w) into the parent configuration (q_P,u+w+z), provided both coordinates of the resulting vector are nonnegative. All vector arithmetic is componentwise. A complete run is a finite rooted tree in which every internal node has exactly two ordered children and obeys one transition, every node carries a configuration with nonnegative counters, and every leaf is labeled (i,(0,0)) for some i∈I. A one-node initial run is allowed. The target is reachable precisely when it labels the root of some complete run. States may repeat, both children may have the same state, and their vectors need not be equal. No separate zero-test operation is available. The system, initial-state list and target are explicit finite inputs; state indices, signed displacement coordinates and nonnegative target coordinates are encoded in binary with separators, and N denotes the resulting bit length. Dimension is fixed at two, while s, the number of transitions and numerical magnitudes vary with the input. Algorithms must give the exact yes/no reachability answer and halt on every valid input. Quantitative bounds should state whether they measure worst-case deterministic Turing-machine time or workspace as a function of N; the source does not select the desired classification or matching-bound precision.
cards.answer_criterion: The surviving research task is to obtain an explicit complexity classification for this binary-encoded reachability problem, beyond the known decidability result and inherited PSPACE hardness. The source does not fix the cost measure or precision needed to count matching upper and lower bounds as a complete answer; this remains a formulation issue. Merely proving decidability again would not settle the original request for precise complexity.

notes: Recovered the original run semantics and binary encoding.

statement_review.remaining_issue: The original asks for precise computational complexity without fixing time versus space, a target class, or the precision required of matching bounds. This revision spells out the natural binary-encoded two-counter extension of its model but does not invent a PSPACE-completeness, elementary-time or other sharper conjecture.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary counter-system reachability follows one sequence of configurations. A branching run is a tree: two independently justified configurations are combined, their resources are added, and a transition applies a fixed displacement. Every leaf must start with zero counters in an allowed initial state. The question asks how difficult it is to recognize whether such a finite justification tree exists.

For example, let i be initial and include transitions (i,i,(1,0),a), (i,i,(0,1),b), and (a,b,(−1,−1),t). The first two create a(1,0) and b(0,1) from zero leaves; the last combines them into t(0,0). Replacing its displacement by (−2,−1) would make that combination invalid because one counter becomes negative. Branching adds the child vectors; it does not copy one vector into both children.

Numerical encoding matters even with only one counter. The original paper proves PSPACE completeness for binary displacements, contrasting it with polynomial-time completeness for unary displacements. The two-counter problem inherits PSPACE hardness by setting every second coordinate to zero. This lower bound alone does not establish PSPACE membership in dimension two.

The 2025 result proves that the reachable configurations in two dimensions have a computable semilinear description. A semilinear set is a finite union of sets b+{k₁p₁+⋯+k_rp_r : k₁,…,k_r∈ℕ}, with fixed nonnegative integer base and period vectors. Such a description gives a terminating reachability decision procedure. The paper explicitly leaves its computational cost unbounded by any stated complexity estimate.

The 2025 presentation permits rules with zero, one or several input states and uses distinct states within each rule. The original binary-tree model fits this setting: zero leaves become initial rules, and a repeated child state can be represented by a fresh copy with the same reachable vectors. This preserves the two counter coordinates. The decidability result therefore applies to the imported problem despite the notational difference.

The original concluding paragraph asked for both decidability and precise complexity. Only the first part is settled by the two-dimensional theorem. This card retains the remaining classification question, while marking its unresolved precision requirement; it is not a new claim that two-dimensional reachability might be undecidable.

A July 2026 preprint claims decidability in general dimension and explicitly leaves complexity upper bounds open. That wider claim is not needed to justify the published two-dimensional result, and it does not provide the missing classification here.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
